title: The site you need before a conference
metaTitle: The page you need before a conference
excerpt: Before a conference, publish one page with one offer and one way to meet. Write it for someone who heard the name once in a loud room.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, one clear subject against a simple ground.
caption: One subject, easy to recognize at a glance. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a conference page contain?
faqs.answer: One page, with the offer, who it is for, and one way to meet. Put the same link on the badge, the slide, and the QR code. Include proof only when it is real, and leave off a logo row you did not earn.

faqs.question: How should someone meet you from that page?
faqs.answer: Pick one path you will actually watch during the event: a calendar, a short form, or a table number and a time. Test it from a phone the day before. Remove the table number the night the event ends so the page does not keep a stale instruction.

faqs.question: What should you leave off a conference page?
faqs.answer: Leave off extra navigation, a second offer, a jobs page in the hero, and motion that delays the sentence. Also leave off live chat unless someone is truly answering. Use the type and color you already have so Monday's site still looks like the same company.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A conference landing page is for a person who heard the name once, in a loud room, and looked it up on a phone in the hallway. The page has one job. Say what you do, who it is for, and how to talk to you while they still remember the conversation. One page, one offer, one way to meet.

Everything else can wait until you are back at a desk. The hallway will not give you a second scroll if the first screen is a manifesto.

## The person in the hallway

They have a badge, a weak connection, and a reason they typed the name. Maybe you said a sentence that matched a problem they have. Maybe a friend pointed at your booth. They do not have your deck. They will not read a history of the company.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) describes the window in ordinary conditions, which the hallway is worse than. People often leave a page in the first 10 to 20 seconds. An average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and readers get through only about a quarter of the words. The research is specific about the bar: to earn a longer look, the value has to be clear within about 10 seconds.

Design for that. The first screen contains the name they heard, the offer in one sentence, and the way to meet. If those three are below a full-screen photograph, you have spent the 10 seconds on a picture. Use a picture if it explains the product. Do not use it as a curtain.

Assume the phone. Large type. A button that is a real button. No hover to reveal the point. Test it on a phone over a cellular connection, not only on the conference wifi, because the wifi will fail at the moment you need it. The page should still say the offer if the images are slow.

Write the sentence the way you say it at the booth, not the way a tagline workshop says it. If you say "we reconcile invoices for clinics," write that. The person is matching your face to a tab. The words should match your mouth.

## One page

One URL. Put it on the badge, the slide, and the card. A homepage plus a product plus a blog plus a careers page is a small website, and it is the wrong instrument for this week. Ship the one page. Add the rest when someone asks for something the page cannot answer.

The page can be long enough to scroll once. It should not be a microsite with its own navigation. Navigation is a choice, and this person should not be choosing among your departments. They should be deciding whether to talk to you.

A reasonable order:

1. Name, offer, and the way to meet.
2. Who it is for, in a sentence, so the wrong people can leave and the right people can stay.
3. What they will see or get, in one picture or a short list of the actual product.
4. Proof you really have: a named pilot, a screenshot of the real product, a client you are allowed to name.
5. The same way to meet, again, at the end.

If you do not have proof, skip the proof section. Do not borrow logos. An empty logo row is worse than no row, because the hallway person has seen a hundred of them today and is using them as a shortcut for "this is not real."

Keep the URL stable through the event. Changing it on the second morning because you thought of a better slug means yesterday's cards are wrong. Pick a boring slug and print it.

## One offer

If you sell three things, pick the one you are here to talk about. Mention the others in a line if you must. Do not give them equal screens. The person will remember one noun. Choose the noun.

The offer should include the next concrete thing, not only the category. "Book a 15-minute slot at the booth" is an offer. "Transform your workflow" is a category. The booth is a physical fact. Use it. Table number, hours, a link to a calendar if the calendar is how you want the meeting to happen. If you would rather they write to you after, say that, and make the mail link obvious. Do not list three equal calls to action. They will pick none.

Pricing, if you have a simple price, can be on the page. It filters the conversations you do not want. If the price is a range you cannot say in public, leave it off and have the conversation. A fake "starting at" number you will not honor is a bad booth memory.

Cut the origin story, the partner logos you barely earned, and the jobs page. None of those help the hallway decision. The jobs page in particular sends a potential customer into a list of roles. Link it from the footer in small type if candidates are also in the building. Do not put it in the first screen.

## One way to meet

Pick the path you will actually watch during the event. A calendar link you check. A short form that lands in an inbox you open. A table number and a time window, if the meeting is physical. One of these.

Test the path the day before, from a phone that is not on your office network. Send one meeting to yourself. If the form needs a login, it is the wrong form. If the calendar is in a timezone you will forget, write the timezone on the page.

Staff the path. A page that asks people to book, while the whole team is on the show floor and nobody confirms, creates a pile of quiet no-shows. Decide who looks at the inbox at lunch and at the end of the day. Write their name on the internal note. The page cannot do that part.

A QR code on the booth should open this exact URL, not your homepage, not a link shortener you will lose the login to. Print the short URL under the code for the person whose camera fails. Test the code at arm's length, in the lighting you will actually have, which is usually worse than your office.

If you are collecting cards instead, the page still matters, because they will look you up after the handshake. The way to meet might then be "write to us with the subject line [event name]." Tell them that on the page so the mail is recognizable in a crowded inbox.

## What to leave off

Leave off the motion that delays the sentence. A loading sequence, a video that autoplays with sound, a cookie wall that covers the offer. The hallway is impatient and the phone is already doing too much. [Google's Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are a sensible bar even for a temporary page: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, layout shift under 0.1. A one-page site in Next.js, or a simple published page, can meet that if you do not bury it in a heavy embed.

Leave off the live chat unless someone is truly watching it. A chat bubble that says you reply instantly, while you are in a session, is a broken promise on the exact day you are making first impressions.

Leave off the "download the deck" button unless the deck can stand alone. Most decks cannot. They are a series of prompts for a speaker who is not in the hallway. If the deck is the leave-behind, make a version that has full sentences. Otherwise the page is the leave-behind.

Do not spin up a new visual system for the event. Use the type and color you already have. A conference is a loud room. Your page should be the quiet, legible object. A special event skin that does not match your real site will confuse the person who visits again on Monday and thinks they have the wrong company.

## After the event

The page can stay up. Change the way to meet. Remove the table number the night the event ends, or the page becomes a small lie for anyone who arrives late. Replace it with the ordinary path: a call, a form, the same offer.

Write to the people you actually spoke with, in the words you used on the page. The page and the follow-up should sound like the same company. If the page said a narrow offer and the email says a broad one, you will feel slick to the person who liked the narrow version.

Keep the URL. It is now a link you have printed and said aloud. Point it at the lasting page rather than deleting it. If the lasting home is a fuller site, this URL can redirect. Do not let it 404 in the week people are sorting business cards.

Then look at what the page had to omit. If the event was also a launch, the next piece of writing is the launch itself, and it should say what changed for the user. A list of internal milestones will not do that. The next piece is [a launch post that is not a press release](/blog/a-launch-post-that-is-not-a-press-release).

Temporary pages and the sites they grow into sit with the rest of Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
